case_name: Fried c. Students' Society of McGill University
text:
Fried c. Students' Society of McGill University

2024 QCCS 1381

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

N° :

500-17-121801-222

DATE :

April 22, 2024

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING :

SERGE
GAUDET, j.s.c.

______________________________________________________________________

JONAH FRIED

Plaintiff

v.

STUDENTS’ SOCIETY OF McGILL UNIVERSITY

-and-

McGILL UNIVERSITY

-and-

SOLIDARITY FOR PALESTINIAN HUMAN RIGHTS

Defendants

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(Motions to dismiss)

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

In the summer of 2022, the Plaintiff, then a McGill student, filed an
Application
Originating a Judicial Proceeding
before this Court. The Application seeks
various declaratory conclusions in relation with a referendum held by the
Students’
Society of McGill University
(“SSMU” or “the Society”) regarding a document
entitled “
Palestine Solidarity Policy
” (“the Policy”). Essentially, the
Plaintiff, who is Jewish, claims that the Policy contravenes the SSMU’s
Constitution and that it is discriminatory.

[
2
]

The Policy was issued and promoted by the
Solidarity for Palestinian
Human Rights (“SPHR”)
, one of the numerous “clubs” (various interest groups
of McGill students) operating under the SSMU Constitution
[1]
.

[
3
]

The SSMU and McGill University ask for the preliminary dismissal of the Plaintiff’s
Application as they consider that the issues it raises are moot and, in any
event, are not founded in law even if the facts alleged were to be taken as
proven. They also argue that the Plaintiff no longer possesses the required
legal interest to pursue the case as he graduated in 2023 and therefore is no
longer a McGill student.

1.

Context

a)

The referendum on the Palestine Solidarity Policy

[
4
]

As its name indicates, the SPHR club is an interest group of the SSMU promoting
and advocating the protection of Palestinians’ fundamental rights. It is also an
advocate of the “BDS” (Boycott/Divestment/Sanctions) movement against the State
of Israel
[2]
.

[
5
]

In February 2022, the SPHR issued the Policy. In essence, the document states
that Palestinians are the victims of a “
settler-colonial apartheid
” that
“
is characterized by a brutal regime of land theft, checkpoints, house
demolitions, environmental destruction, deportation and extrajudicial killings
at the hands of soldiers, police and settlers
”. The resolution that the Policy
was proposing would oblige the SSMU, for a period of five years: 1) to issue, once
a semester, a public statement affirming its “
solidarity with Palestinian
students and with Palestinian liberation from settler-colonial apartheid
”;
2) to “
completely boycott all corporations and institutions complicit in
settler-colonial apartheid against Palestinians
” and 3) to “
campaign for
a complete divestment of the University from these corporations or institutions
”
[3]
.

[
6
]

The Policy was the topic of a referendum held by the SSMU in March 2022.
The question put by the SSMU to the McGill students was the following:
“Do
you agree to the SSMU’s adoption of the Palestine Solidarity Policy?”
.

[
7
]

The Plaintiff, who is Jewish and describes himself as a Zionist, was an
active participant of the “No” campaign.

[
8
]

On March 21, 2022, the results of the referendum were issued: 2,294
students voted in favor of the Policy (71.1%) and 934 students voted against it
(28.9%). According to the SSMU, the turn-out for the vote was approximately 16.5%
of the eligible voters, above the 15% quorum established by the regulations.

b)

Reactions of the University and of the SSMU’s Board of directors

[
9
]

On March 22, 2022, the day after the referendum results were known, the
Deputy Provost for the Student life and learning of the University, Mr. Fabrice
Labeau, sent a letter to the president of the SSMU
[4]
.
Mr. Lareau indicated that the Policy was in essence a repetition of previous
questions that had been judged against SSMU’s Constitution, which obliges the
Society “
to act in the best interests of [its] members as a whole
”. He
also mentioned that the Policy is conducive to discrimination based on race,
national or ethnic origin and religion.

[
10
]

The
purpose of that letter was to constitute a notice of default under the 2019 Memorandum
of Agreement between the University and the SSMU, which deals notably with the
collection by the University of the students’ financial contributions to the
SSMU
[5]
.
Mr. Labeau concluded his letter by stating that the SSMU had 30 days to repeal
the Policy, failing which the 2019 Memorandum of Agreement with the University would
be terminated.

[
11
]

On
March 24, Mr. Labeau, in a statement addressed this time to the whole McGill
community, reiterated that “
initiatives such as [the Policy], […] create
excessive polarization in our community, encourage a culture of ostracization
and disrespect due to students’ identity, religious or political beliefs, and
are in contradiction with the University’s values of inclusion, diversity and
respect
.” He added that “
they are also in contradiction with the
principles expressed by SSMU in its own constitution
”
[6]
.

[
12
]

On
April 25, 2022, the Board of directors of the SSMU released a statement,
explaining why it had decided
not
to adopt the Policy
[7]
:

The Board of directors has determined that the
Palestine Solidarity Policy is not in conformity with the SSMU Constitution,
the SSMU Equity Policy, the 2016 SSMU Judicial Board ruling in Reference re
Legality of the BDS Motion and similar Motions, and Quebec law.

As per Section 6.1 of the SSMU Constitution, all
motions passed by Referendum must be ratified by the Board of Directors prior
to being formally adopted by the SSMU. Given that Palestine Solidarity Policy
does not conform with numerous SSMU Governing Documents, the Board cannot
ratify the Policy. As such the
Palestine Solidarity Policy will not be
adopted by the SSMU
.

c)      The
judicial proceedings filed by Plaintiff and the Motions to dismiss

[
13
]

On
July 22, 2022, despite the position taken by the SSMU’s Board of Directors, the
Plaintiff filed the judicial Application that is the object of the present
debate.

[
14
]

Arguing
that the Policy is in violation of the SSMU’s Constitution and other internal
by-laws, that it is against McGill University policy against discrimination and
Quebec law, and alleging that it provoked an increased number of antisemitic
attacks on the Jewish students of the University after its issuance and during
the referendum campaign, the Plaintiff is seeking various declarative conclusions
from the Court.

[
15
]

More
precisely, he is asking the Superior Court to declare that:

i) the referendum vote held in March 2022 is
contrary to the Constitution, by-laws and policies of the SSMU;

ii) the said referendum gives rise to no rights,
obligations or actions;

iii) the Memorandum of Agreement with the
University prohibits the SSMU from enacting discriminatory policies like the
Policy and to benefit from the Memorandum of Agreement with the University
should the SSMU violate its constitution, by-laws or policies;

iv) the Policy is discriminatory, biased and
antisemitic;

v)  he has the right to enforce the Constitution,
by-laws and policies of the SSMU and the right to rely on the Memorandum of
Agreement as he is a student and a member of the SSMU;

vi) the Policy and its derivatives and the BDS
movement violate article 3 of the Act respecting Academic Freedom in the
University sector.

[
16
]

After
the Plaintiff filed his proceeding, the SSMU and the University each filed a
Motion to dismiss, their main argument being that the whole issue is moot as
the Board of Directors of the SSMU decided not to adopt the Policy. They also
claim that the issue is not justiciable considering its political nature and that
the affairs of the SSMU should be under the exclusive control of its Board of
Directors without undue interference by its members.

d)      Procedural evolution of the Application

[
17
]

These
Motions to dismiss were scheduled to be heard in the Spring of 2023, but their
presentation was postponed twice. They were finally to be heard on November 16
and 17, 2023.

[
18
]

A
week before that date, the Plaintiff notified a re-modified Application
[8]
.
The modifications were twofold. First, another student was added as a
co-Plaintiff (Mr. Cody Benjamin Tanentzap) as Mr. Fried had graduated and was no
longer a McGill Student. Second, allegations were added with respect to another
policy of the same ilk that was to be put to a referendum to the McGill
students in the fall of 2023, namely the “Policy against Genocide in Palestine”,
in the wake of the events that provoked the war between Israel and the Hamas in
the Gaza strip.

[
19
]

It
is relevant to mention that injunctive proceedings have also been introduced
before the Superior Court last Fall to prohibit the holding of the referendum
on that new Palestine policy
[9]
,
and that Me Michael Bergman, who is representing the Plaintiff in the present
case, is also the lawyer acting on behalf on the plaintiff (whose name is
confidential) in that other case.

[
20
]

On
November 16, Justice Yves Poirier noted that the Plaintiff’s modifications to
its application were contested by the SSMU. He also indicated that, in his
view, it was not possible to add a new plaintiff by way of a modification to
the proceeding.  The Plaintiff’s lawyer then announced that Mr. Tanentzap would
rather proceed via an aggressive voluntary intervention to enter the case. Justice
Poirier reluctantly accepted another postponement of the hearing on the Motions
to dismiss to permit the filing of the announced intervention, but expressly
indicated that it needed to be submitted before November 24, 2023, under sanction
of foreclosure. He then fixed the hearing of the Motions to dismiss to April 3
and 4, 2024.

[
21
]

The
Plaintiff did not respect the delay fixed by Justice Poirier to file the
intervention. It was only notified to the Defendants on November 27, 2023.
Neither did he comply with the delays prescribed by law to file his motion to
modify his proceedings, as that motion was only filed on April 1
st
,
2024 (a holiday) for the April 3 hearing, short of the 3-day period set forth
in art. 101 of the
Code of Civil procedure
.

[
22
]

Considering
all the circumstances, I decided that both the intervention and the Plaintiff’s
sought modifications would not be authorized, as they had not been filed in a
timely fashion
[10]
.

[
23
]

Consequently,
the Motions to dismiss are to be decided in light of the Plaintiff’s
Modified
Application originating a judicial Proceeding
dated August 11, 2023.

2.

Analysis

[
24
]

As
stated above, the principal argument of the SSMU and McGill to have the
Plaintiff’s Application dismissed at a preliminary stage is mootness. They
claim that the litigation has never had any
substratum
considering that
the SSMU’s Board of directors decided not to adopt the Policy despite the
results of the referendum.

[
25
]

Article
10, third paragraph of the
Code of Civil Procedure
mentions that “
the
courts are not required to decide theoretical questions
”.

[
26
]

This
is in line with the principles enunciated by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Borowski
v. Canada (Attorney General)
[11]

. In that judgment, the Supreme Court ruled that courts should refuse to hear
cases for which there is no live issue between the parties, unless there are
good reasons to decide otherwise
[12]
.

[
27
]

The
Supreme Court established a two-step analysis when mootness is alleged.

[
28
]

First,
it is necessary to determine if the case is indeed moot, that is to say, “
whether
the required tangible and concrete dispute has disappeared, and the issues have
become academic
”.

[
29
]

Secondly,
if the case is moot, the court must whether it should exercise its discretion
to hear it anyway. This requires an analysis of the following elements, all
linked to the foundations of the general rule not to hear moot cases
[13]
:
1)
the presence of an adversarial context
: despite the mootness of the
issue, is there still an adversarial context to ensure that the issues would be
well and fully argued by parties who have somehow a stake in the outcome?
[14]
;
2)
the concerns regarding judicial economy
: is it a situation where the moot
case should be heard despite the usual concerns regarding the use of scarce
judicial resources?
[15]

and 3)
the need for proper law-making function by the courts
: could a
decision on the moot issue be useful in the elaboration of the law, where such
elaboration can be made by the courts in the respect of their constitutional
role?
[16]

[
30
]

Applying
these principles and criteria to the case at hand, I am of the view that the
Plaintiff’s Application must be dismissed as the issues it raised are entirely
theoretical.

[
31
]

First,
as the SSMU’s Board of directors decided not to adopt the Policy, there is no
live issue between the parties. In essence, the Plaintiff considers that the
Policy contravenes the SSMU’s constitution and the law, notably as it is
discriminatory against the Jewish students. This is also the position of the
University, described in the Deputy Provost Labeau in his March 22, 2022,
letter to the president of the SSMU and in the declaration to the same effect
addressed to the whole McGill community two days later. Finally, it is also the
position of the SSMU whose Board of Directors has decided not to adopt the
Policy precisely because it contravenes its own constitution and Quebec law.

[
32
]

In
these circumstances, it is difficult to see that any “live issue” ever existed
for the present litigation. As rightly pointed out by the SSMU, we are faced here
with a case where a live issue existed at the outset of a judicial proceeding
but disappeared afterwards, it is rather a situation where the issues raised by
the Plaintiff’s judicial application were moot from the start before the
application was filed. The mootness doctrine hence applies with even more force
than in the usual situation where the “live issue” ceased to exist while the
instance was pending.

[
33
]

At
the hearing, Plaintiff took the position that the issues raised in his judicial
application are not moot, because the Policy is technically “in force” despite
not having been adopted by the SSMU’s Board of directors. This argument stems
from the fact that the SSMU regulations of referenda distinguish referenda,
where the result would be binding on the SSMU, and plebiscites, which are
expressly declared non-binding by the regulations
[17]
.

[
34
]

I
admit being a bit puzzled by this position of the Plaintiff. He argues that the
Policy is “in force” despite not having been adopted by the SSMU’s Board of
Directors so that the courts would be justified to declare that it is void as
it contravenes the SSMU’s Constitution and the law. In other words, the
Plaintiff is asking the Superior Court to consider that the Policy creates
legal consequences, so that the issue is not moot, for the sake of having the same
Superior court declare thereafter that the said Policy is void
ab initio

and therefore does not create any legal consequences.

[
35
]

That
said, I fail to see how this distinction between referenda and plebiscites can
change the fact that, in the case at hand, the Policy has absolutely no real
and concrete consequences for any McGill student as the Board of Directors of the
SSMU has decided not to adopt it and is acting accordingly. It is as if a
person were attacking as unconstitutional a bill that has not been adopted by
the legislature: it seems obvious that no judicial resources should be devoted
to such a “case”.

[
36
]

In
the present situation the SSMU’s Board of Directors, which manages the affairs
of the SSMU both according to the law
[18]

and the SSMU’s constitution
[19]
,
resolved not to adopt the Policy and that decision is not attacked by the
Plaintiff or by anyone else. In these circumstances, it is difficult to see how
there could be a live issue in respect of the said Policy which do not create
any concrete consequences for the SSMU or anyone.

[
37
]

Finally,
I add that, with respect to the specific conclusion seeking those future policies
“like” the Policy be declared in contravention of the 2019 Memorandum of
Agreement between the SSMU and the University, it seems even clearer that the
said conclusion raises an issue that cannot be the object of a judicial
proceeding. Courts cannot, nor should they try, to assess whether a policy or
resolution that has not been yet issued is illegal or contravenes a contract or
a law. They are not required to answer questions without a proper factual basis
and context. The rule stated in the third paragraph of art. 10 CCP applies with
even more force to questions that are not only theoretical, but also entirely
hypothetical
[20]
.

[
38
]

I
am therefore of the view that the issues raised by the Plaintiff’s judicial
application in respect of the Policy are moot.

0-0-0

[
39
]

The
second part of the analysis is to determine whether the present case should be
heard even though the issues it raises are moot
[21]
.

[
40
]

I
am of the view that it should not.

[
41
]

First,
we are not dealing here with a situation where the issue is moot but that,
nonetheless, there remains a context for a serious adversarial debate. There
are simply no consequences flowing from the Policy as the latter was not
adopted by the Board of Directors of the SSMU and as all the parties before me
agree that the Policy should be considered illegal and non-existent because it contravenes
the SSMU’s constitution and is discriminatory.

[
42
]

Second,
it would not appear appropriate to devote precious judicial resources to the
present litigation, which is moot, while the legality and validity of a similar
policy is presently before the Superior Court in the other case mentioned
above. While that other proceeding is for the issuance of an injunction to
prevent the holding of a referendum on the “Policy against genocide in
Palestine” rather than for declarative relief, the legal issues that are at
play in both cases are virtually the same, if not identical, and they are
argued by the same lawyer who is acting for the Plaintiff in the present case.
From the standpoint of judicial economy, it is better that the issues be
debated in that other case.

[
43
]

Third,
it must be underlined that, on their face, the issues raised by the Plaintiff
in the present proceedings are more of a political than of a legal nature. The
debate is best left to the political institutions in place at McGill. The usual
reluctance of the courts to interfere in the internal affairs of a university
or a students’ association (unless an illegality is shown to exist
[22]
)
is even more relevant in a situation where the issues at stake are moot and
where the policy attacked does not create any real or concrete consequences for
anyone.

0-0-0

[
44
]

Considering
the above, it is not necessary to address the issue of Plaintiff’s legal
interest. Even if had the required interest to pursue the case– which is
certainly not clear
[23]
–,
that does not change the fact that the issues raised are moot.

[
45
]

Moreover,
as both the SSMU and McGill mentioned at the hearing that they were not asking
the Court to declare Plaintiff’s recourse abusive if it was dismissed due to mootness,
that question need not be examined either.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
46
]

GRANTS

the
Motion by the Students’ Society of McGill University to Dismiss the
Application originating a Judicial proceeding
dated December 2, 2022;

[
47
]

GRANTS

the
Motion of McGill University to Dismiss the ‘Application Originating a
Judicial Proceeding”
dated January 11, 2023;

[
48
]

DISMISSES

the
Plaintiff’s Re-modified Application Originating a Judicial Proceeding
dated
August 11, 2023;

[
49
]

THE
WHOLE,
with judicial costs.

Superior Court to exercise its discretion to hear his case if it were found to
be moot, as he rather argued that the case was not moot. I consider, however,

lawyer.

review proceeding where he alleges that his rights were not respected by one of
the university’s comittee (par.139 and ff.). But it could be argued that the
situation is not the same where a former student is seeking declarative
conclusions based on the constitution and by-laws or contracts of the students’
association, he is no more a member.
